segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: From WBEZ Chicago, it's This American Life. I'm Ira Glass. OK, so maybe you saw in the news that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has ordered everybody in the Armed Services over 30 years old to have their testosterone levels tested. That's men and women, both. And then anybody who wants to get special shots to get testosterone boost, they can get them.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: The goal here-- Hegseth's social media post about this was titled The High T-- High Testosterone-- Department of War. And maybe you saw. People who had all kinds of reactions to this, including lots of people joking about how Hegseth was suddenly embracing gender-affirming care.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: I personally had a strong reaction to the idea of testing everybody's testosterone levels in a workplace, which was, I've lived through that here at my job at This American Life. We did that back in 2002. We did a show where we talked about testosterone and the personality traits that supposedly go along with higher testosterone levels.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And as part of that show, all of us on staff got our testosterone levels tested to see who had the highest. And then before the results came back, we all sat down and discussed who we thought might have the highest. And then we revealed the results.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Anyway, today, as a cautionary tale to the men and women of the Armed Services about what it's like for an entire workplace to test their testosterone, we are rerunning that old show. Our staff experiment, you'll hear, comes up a little ways into the show. It's Act Two. But the original episode started with one of our producers at the time, Alex Blumberg, joining me in the studio to explain why we took up the subject in the first place back in 2002.

segments.speaker: Alex Blumberg
segments.text: Hello, Ira.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Alex.

segments.speaker: Alex Blumberg
segments.text: Yes?

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: What's the reason for this week's show?

segments.speaker: Alex Blumberg
segments.text: Well, I've been thinking about that. And for me, the reason for today's program goes back to a book I read when I was 15 called The Women's Room. Maybe people listening will remember The Women's Room. It was sort of a seminal feminist novel from the '70s.

segments.speaker: Alex Blumberg
segments.text: And I first came across The Women's Room when I was digging through my parents' bookshelves looking for porn, books with naughty parts in them, like Fear of Flying. And so I picked it up, and I read it.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Because the word "women" was in the title.

segments.speaker: Alex Blumberg

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And I noticed you happen to have brought into the studio with you today a copy of The Women's Room.

segments.speaker: Alex Blumberg
segments.text: Yeah, well, I recently reread it just to see. For example, I bookmarked a couple of these things. On page 198, the narrator comes in. And she says, "You think I hate men. I guess I do."

segments.speaker: Alex Blumberg
segments.text: And then a little bit further down, she says, "My feelings about men are the result of my experience. I have little sympathy for them. Like a Jew just released from Dachau, I watched the handsome young Nazi soldier fall writhing to the ground with a bullet in his stomach. And I look briefly and walk on. I don't even need to shrug. I simply don't care."

segments.speaker: Alex Blumberg
segments.text: And then a little bit later, "My hatred is learned from experience. That is not prejudice. I wish it were prejudice. Then, perhaps, I could unlearn it."

segments.speaker: Alex Blumberg
segments.text: There's not very much pornographic about that.

segments.speaker: Alex Blumberg
segments.text: It's an incredibly strange thing to read this book at that age. Because at that age, I felt like there's one other woman who comes into play at this point. And I probably shouldn't say her name. Let's just call her Kelly.

segments.speaker: Alex Blumberg
segments.text: And she was in eighth grade with me. And she sat two rows away from me. And I remember, one time, sitting in homeroom with her and seeing her button-down shirt was open a little bit. And I could catch the bare sliver of her little training bra.

segments.speaker: Alex Blumberg
segments.text: And it was perhaps the most desire I've ever felt in my life, maybe. It was, like, all consuming. And I couldn't concentrate for the rest of the day. I remember it to this day.

segments.speaker: Alex Blumberg
segments.text: And so, at the time I was reading this book, I felt like, oh, my God. I could see myself becoming the people that she was describing, the men she was describing. And it was really terrifying.

segments.speaker: Alex Blumberg
segments.text: My testosterone and how it affects me and how I react to it, I think about on a daily basis, all the time. It often feels like there's something in my body giving me instructions that I probably shouldn't follow.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: OK, which brings us to today's program. A while back, Alex tried to convince all of us who work on the radio show that we should do an entire program about testosterone. And I have to say, none of us were really buying it, especially the women, who found the subject dull, even though, as Alex tried to point out to them, women have testosterone, and it affects them pretty much exactly the same way that it affects men.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: I think all of us were fearing a kind of "men are from Mars, women are from Venus" sort of thing, how hormones make men be all aggressive and women all nonaggressive in very stereotyped ways, which all seem kind of reductionistic and dumb headed. And then Alex started reading and calling people. And one of the people that he called was this guy who wrote an article for GQ Magazine about what happened to him when, because of medical reasons, he stopped producing testosterone. And for four months, he lived without testosterone before they caught the problem. And the way he described living without testosterone was really incredible.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: Everything that I identify as being me-- my ambition, my interest in things, my sense of humor, the inflection in my voice-- the quality of my speech even changed in the time that I was without a lot of the hormone. So yes, the introduction of testosterone returned everything. There were things that I find offensive about my own personality that were disconnected then. And it was nice to be without them.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: Envy, the desire to judge itself-- I approached people with a humility that I had never displayed before. I grew up in a culture, like all of us, that divides the soul from the body, and that that is your singleness. That is your uniqueness.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: And then I go through this experience where I have small amounts of a bodily chemical removed and then reintroduced. And it changes everything I know as my self. And it violates the sanctity of that understanding. And that's humbling. And it's terrifying.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: I think, when it comes to this stuff, most of us do not know what to believe. We're caught between thinking that our hormones and body chemistry can determine so much about our personalities and wanting to believe that they don't. And so today on our program, we bring you four stories exploring that question.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: How much does testosterone determine? Act One of our show, Infinite Gent-- someone gets pumped up with several times the amount of testosterone that most men have and describe some surprising changes. Act Two, Contest-osterone. In that act, at Alex's suggestion, all of us on the staff of this radio program decide to find out who has the most and who has the least testosterone, with lab tests, to see how the levels match with our personality traits-- an exercise, I have to say, most of us at this point would not recommend that you try at your workplace or with your friends.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Act Three, Life at Zero, in which we hear about what it means to lose all your testosterone. Act Four, Learning to Shut Up-- in that act, a mother asks her teenage son all her questions about what it means to be a boy, which is, of course, exactly of thing you do not want your mother asking you on tape at 15. Stay with us.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: It's This American Life, act one, Infinite Gent. So what exactly does an injection of testosterone do to you? What kind of changes do you feel? Back in 2002, when we first broadcast today's show, our producer, Alex Blumberg, talked with Griffin Hansbury about that experience. Griffin got massive testosterone shots as part of transitioning from female to male, which Griffin did after he got out of college.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: I should tell you that, because it's been over 20 years since this interview happened, you might notice some ideas about gender and some language that are of its time. Also, a quick heads-up to listeners that the interview acknowledges the existence of sex and sexual desire.

segments.speaker: Griffin Hansbury
segments.text: I went to Bryn Mawr College, which is a women's college, and chose a women's college because I strongly identified as a woman at the time, as a feminist, and as a dyke. I had my leather biker jacket and my big leather belt and my black T-shirts and my Doc Marten boots, my combat boots. And that felt pretty comfortable for a while.

segments.speaker: Griffin Hansbury
segments.text: And then, my sophomore year in college, I was lying in bed with my girlfriend. I don't know if we were talking or what it was. And it just sort of hit me like a bolt of lightning, as they say. And I just knew that I had to change my body.

segments.speaker: Griffin Hansbury
segments.text: And so I started doing the research on it. And the only way to do that was to take testosterone. My first injection was a pretty large one of 2 cc's of 200 milligram strength depo testosterone, which is a fairly high amount. Just to give you a sense of how much that is, the average amount of testosterone in an average male body is between 300 and 1,000 nanograms per deciliter of blood.

segments.speaker: Griffin Hansbury
segments.text: After that shot, and after an average shot, my testosterone levels go up to over 2,000 nanograms per deciliter so that I have the testosterone of two high-testosterone men in my body at once.

segments.speaker: Alex Blumberg
segments.text: You have the testosterone of two linebackers.

segments.speaker: Griffin Hansbury
segments.text: Exactly.

segments.speaker: Alex Blumberg
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Griffin Hansbury
segments.text: Exactly. That's a lot. It's a lot of T. And what's amazing about it is how instantaneous it is, that it happens within a few days, really. The world just changes.

segments.speaker: Alex Blumberg
segments.text: What were some of the changes that you didn't expect?

segments.speaker: Griffin Hansbury
segments.text: The most overwhelming feeling is the incredible increase in libido and change in the way that I perceived women and the way I thought about sex. Before testosterone, I would be riding the subway, which is the traditional hotbed of lust in the city. And I would see a woman on the subway. And I would think, she's attractive. I'd like to meet her. What's that book she's reading? If I could talk to her, this is what I would say. There would be a narrative. There would be this stream of language. It would be very verbal.

segments.speaker: Griffin Hansbury
segments.text: After testosterone, there was no narrative. There was no language whatsoever. It was just I would see a woman who was attractive or not attractive. She might have an attractive quality, nice ankles or something. And the rest of her would be fairly unappealing to me. But that was enough to basically just flood my mind with aggressive pornographic images, just one after another. It was like being in a pornographic movie house in my mind.

segments.speaker: Griffin Hansbury
segments.text: And I couldn't turn it off. I could not turn it off. Everything I looked at, everything I touched, turned to sex. I was an editorial assistant. And I would be standing at the Xerox machine. And this big, shuddering, warm, inanimate object would just drive me crazy. It was very, very erotic to me.

segments.speaker: Alex Blumberg
segments.text: (LAUGHING) The Xerox machine.

segments.speaker: Griffin Hansbury
segments.text: The Xerox machine or a car. I would see-- I remember walking up 5th Avenue one day. And this red convertible went by. It was a Mustang. And I remember just getting this jolt in my pants, this very physical, visceral, sexual reaction to seeing a red convertible.

segments.speaker: Alex Blumberg
segments.text: What did you do with that? What did you think?

segments.speaker: Griffin Hansbury
segments.text: [SCOFFS] Well, I felt like a monster a lot of the time. And it made me understand men. It made me understand adolescent boys a lot. Suddenly, hair is sprouting, and I'm turning into this beast. And I would really berate myself for it.

segments.speaker: Griffin Hansbury
segments.text: I remember walking up 5th Avenue. There was a woman walking in front of me. And she was wearing this little skirt and this little top. And I was looking at her ass. And I kept saying to myself, don't look at it. Don't look at it. And I kept looking at it. And I walked past her. And this voice in my head kept saying, turn around to look at her breasts. Turn around. Turn around. Turn around.

segments.speaker: Griffin Hansbury
segments.text: And my feminist, female background kept saying, don't you dare, you pig. Don't turn around. And I fought myself for a whole block. And then I turned around and checked her out. And before, it was cool. When I would do a poetry reading, I would get up, and I would read these poems about women on the street. And I was a butch dyke. And that was very, very cutting edge. And that was very sexy and raw. And now I'm just a jerk.

segments.speaker: Griffin Hansbury
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Griffin Hansbury
segments.text: So I do feel like I've lost this edge, this nice, sort of avant garde kind of-- and I've gotten into a lot of arguments with women friends, co-workers who did not know about my past as a female. I call myself a post-feminist. And I had a woman say, you're not a post-feminist. You're a misogynist.

segments.speaker: Griffin Hansbury
segments.text: And I said, that's impossible. I can't be a misogynist. And I couldn't explain to her how I had come to this point in my life. And to her, I was just a misogynist. And that's unfortunate because it's a lot more complicated than that.

segments.speaker: Alex Blumberg
segments.text: [LAUGHS] I'll say. Wow. Testosterone didn't just turn you into a man. It turned you into Rush Limbaugh.

segments.speaker: Griffin Hansbury
segments.text: I know. That, I was not expecting. That, I was not expecting. So I had to relearn how to talk to women. And I had to learn how to rephrase things, how to hold my tongue on certain things. And I'm not very good at it, so I get in trouble.

segments.speaker: Alex Blumberg
segments.text: That is so fascinating. Because as a man, I think, from the time I went through puberty, I feel like that's something that I've been learning to do in a certain way-- is just figure out how to say things without getting myself in trouble.

segments.speaker: Alex Blumberg
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Griffin Hansbury
segments.text: Right. Yeah. Yeah.

segments.speaker: Alex Blumberg
segments.text: I would not have thought that you would have had that problem.

segments.speaker: Griffin Hansbury
segments.text: Right. Because I should know better or something.

segments.speaker: Alex Blumberg
segments.text: Or something. Other than the visual and other than the libidinal, are there other ways that you feel like testosterone has altered the way you feel or perceive?

segments.speaker: Griffin Hansbury
segments.text: Something that happened after I started taking testosterone-- I became interested in science. I was never interested in science before.

segments.speaker: Alex Blumberg
segments.text: No way. Come on. Are you serious?

segments.speaker: Alex Blumberg
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Griffin Hansbury
segments.text: I'm serious. I'm serious.

segments.speaker: Alex Blumberg
segments.text: You're just setting us back a hundred years, sir.

segments.speaker: Griffin Hansbury
segments.text: I know I am I know.

segments.speaker: Griffin Hansbury
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Griffin Hansbury
segments.text: Again, I have to have this caveat in here. I cannot say it was the testosterone. All I can say is that this interest happened after T. There's BT and AT. And this was definitely After T. And I became interested in science. I found myself understanding physics in a way I never had before.

segments.speaker: Griffin Hansbury
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Griffin Hansbury
segments.text: It's true. It's true.

segments.speaker: Alex Blumberg
segments.text: Wow.

segments.speaker: Griffin Hansbury
segments.text: I did.

segments.speaker: Alex Blumberg
segments.text: How about in the way you feel things and in the way you perceive of your feelings? Is there any change there?

segments.speaker: Griffin Hansbury
segments.text: [SIGHS] I have a hard time crying. It's very difficult for me to cry. And before testosterone, it was great to, if I was frustrated or angry or sad, have a good cry. You'd feel better afterwards. And I do wonder if there isn't a chemical component behind it. Because I now have a hard time doing it. And it's very frustrating.

segments.speaker: Griffin Hansbury
segments.text: And what I will do is, when I feel that pressure build up, I'll go into my room. I'll close the door and force myself. I have to force myself to cry. And the quality of the crying is different than the quality of the crying was before T. It's very dry. I find myself sort of moaning and sobbing but with very little tears.

segments.speaker: Alex Blumberg
segments.text: You have answered a lot of questions for us today.

segments.speaker: Alex Blumberg
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Alex Blumberg
segments.text: And reinforced a lot of stereotypes that we've almost disspelled with.

segments.speaker: Griffin Hansbury
segments.text: I know.

segments.speaker: Griffin Hansbury
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Griffin Hansbury
segments.text: I know I have. I know it.

segments.speaker: Alex Blumberg
segments.text: Did you have an idea of what kind of man you were going to be before the transition; this is my model?

segments.speaker: Griffin Hansbury
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Alex Blumberg
segments.text: What was it?

segments.speaker: Griffin Hansbury
segments.text: I used to watch a lot of Beverly Hills 90210. And Jason Priestley was my ideal, at least physically. I wanted sideburns so bad. And that was the first facial hair that came in. I got these beautiful sideburns. So it was sort of like the James Dean, Jason Priestley kind of model, I think. That didn't quite materialize. I was better at that as a dyke than I am as a man, I have to say.

segments.speaker: Alex Blumberg
segments.text: [LAUGHS]

segments.speaker: Alex Blumberg
segments.text: And how do you feel about that?

segments.speaker: Griffin Hansbury
segments.text: It's a bit of a disappointment. It's a bit of a disappointment. I often ask people, what kind of a guy am I? What do you see? And unfortunately, people often respond that they see a nerd, which I never was before. I was always really kind of cool and popular and hip and whatever. And now I'm 5 foot 4. And I work out, but I'm not real muscular. And I'm pretty small.

segments.speaker: Griffin Hansbury
segments.text: I'm pale skinned. And my hair is starting to thin. And I've got glasses. And of course, I'm also a sensitive guy now. I used to be the butch dyke. And I was seen as very aggressive. And I was more masculine in many ways, outwardly, anyway, before testosterone. And now I don't have to prove anything. So I can lay back and talk with my hands and all that stuff that you're not supposed to do.

segments.speaker: Griffin Hansbury
segments.text: So I'm still very much learning how to be a man in the world. There's a lot to learn. Men-- walking the street is a constant battle. It's a constant contest.

segments.speaker: Griffin Hansbury
segments.text: I began to notice, once I started to pass as a man, that single men walking alone down the street will veer away from their path to walk towards me, get in my space, and then veer back. And it's very much like a little aggressive move. I've had men, just angry guys, walking on the street, just body check me. So I really feel like I have to sort of puff myself up so that people will keep their distance a little bit. But if I'm off guard and I'm walking around and I'm enjoying the scenery, it's pretty much guaranteed that somebody will shove me.

segments.speaker: Alex Blumberg
segments.text: Were there specific things that you were hoping for?

segments.speaker: Griffin Hansbury
segments.text: I think that the main thing that you hope for, that one hopes for, and that I hope for when starting testosterone, was to pass as male, to be perceived by the world as a man. But I do have a sort of love, hate relationship with passing, that my whole deeper self becomes invisible, and my history becomes invisible. And I think that's hard. It's a hard place to be.

segments.speaker: Alex Blumberg
segments.text: Right, right.

segments.speaker: Griffin Hansbury
segments.text: Especially because, when I got my first job as a man, they didn't know anything about my past. It was very corporate. So I had to let go of any edgy clothing and facial hair and whatnot that I had before. And I became really boring. I felt like, wow, people must think I'm really boring. If they only knew that I'm so fascinating.

segments.speaker: Griffin Hansbury
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Griffin Hansbury
segments.text: Throughout those almost four years, I had to conceal a lot. I would lie about where I went to college, because I went to Bryn Mawr. And I couldn't say I went to Bryn Mawr.

segments.speaker: Alex Blumberg
segments.text: What college did you say you went to?

segments.speaker: Griffin Hansbury
segments.text: [CHUCKLES] Well, Bryn Mawr is in the bi-college relationship with Haverford College. And so I would say I went to Haverford, which is kind of-- I don't want to say anything bad about Haverford. Some of my best friends went there.

segments.speaker: Griffin Hansbury
segments.text: But I think Bryn Mawr is a superior school to Haverford. I do. And I think it's a superior education. And when I have to say I went to Haverford, it's like a little knife in my heart.

segments.speaker: Griffin Hansbury
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Griffin Hansbury
segments.text: But no offense to my Haverford friends.

segments.speaker: Alex Blumberg
segments.text: [LAUGHS] What do you feel the biggest thing that you do miss is?

segments.speaker: Griffin Hansbury
segments.text: Hmm. Maybe the close relationships that I had with women. I still have close relationships with the women I've known since before T. But I don't make close relationships with new female friends. It's hard to do. There's a barrier.

segments.speaker: Griffin Hansbury
segments.text: So I kind of miss being part of a cool bunch of women. I actually like women better than men. It just so happens that I fit in more as a man. But I think women are really cool. Sisterhood is powerful, all that stuff.

segments.speaker: Alex Blumberg
segments.text: [CHUCKLES] Yeah. Yeah. And what do you think is the biggest thing you've gained?

segments.speaker: Griffin Hansbury
segments.text: Biggest thing I've gained-- it's just so great when people call me sir. Even after seven years, I don't always hear it. But it still rings a little bell inside my heart-- like, oh, sir. It's wonderful. And it's something that, when I was a little kid, I used to wish for. Turn me into a boy-- Pinocchio. And you never really think it's possible. But it is possible.

segments.speaker: Griffin Hansbury
segments.text: And the other nice thing about it is, knowing that that's possible, that you can actually make this enormous leap means that, well, then anything else must be possible, too. Because this is certainly unbelievable.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Griffin Hansbury is a psychoanalyst and the author of the novel, Some Strange Music Draws Me In. That conversation with Alex Blumberg happened over 20 years ago during his early transition back in 2002. When we reached out to him today, he told us that he would describe some of these experiences differently now, the way he talked about gender and also the way he talked about looking at women's bodies.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: In retrospect, he says, it wasn't just the testosterone affecting him when he was looking at women. He says he'd also absorbed a lot of very traditional messages about masculinity. Overall, he said, he wouldn't want listeners to come away thinking that testosterone by itself explains so much about men's relationships with women and so much about desire.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass

segments.speaker: Man

segments.text: It wasn't that I was behaving. It was that I was not behaving at all. I was, when I was awake, literally sitting in bed and staring at the wall with neither interest nor disinterest for three, four hours at a time. If you'd had a camera in the room, you would have thought I was comatose. I would go out. I would buy some groceries early in the morning. And that would be it. My day had no content.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: I had no interest in even watching TV, much less reading the newspaper or a book. Food-- I didn't want my food to taste good or interesting. And when you're blessed with that lack of desire, you can eat a loaf of Wonder Bread with mayonnaise. And that will be your day.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: And I only saw my girlfriend on weekends, since she was living in New York and I was living in Philly. So I could get away with it five days at a time. And needless to say, there was absolutely no desire.

segments.text: Act Four, Learning to Shut Up. OK, so we started today's program with my coworker, Alex, remembering what it was like to be a 15-year-old boy. And we're going to end it now with another 15-year-old boy, someone who's experiencing the years when a boy's body is flooded with 10 or 20 times the hormones he has in early childhood or more. segments.speaker: Miriam Toews
segments.text: First off, his hair is red and shaggy and longish. And he's pale and slim and 6 feet tall. Music is everything to him, which makes sense, because he's 15. I was 22 when he was born. I'd never had brothers or any close male relatives. And I'd always dreamed of having a brother or a son. The idea of having a boy in my family was strange and exotic.

segments.speaker: Miriam Toews
segments.text: When he was born, it was like I had given birth to a llama or something. All my girlfriends came to visit me and him in the hospital. And I took them down to the second floor nursery. And we stared at him in awe from behind a glass window. That's him, I said, with the orange fuzz on his head. He was lying naked and spread-eagled under a bright heat lamp. He seemed very content.

segments.speaker: Miriam Toews
segments.text: My friend, Carol, gasped and said, oh, my God, he's got the biggest balls I've ever seen in my life. We all started laughing our heads off. And then the nurse came and told us his scrotum would shrink to normal size in a few days. I haven't seen him naked in years. But it still often feels, when I look at him, that I'm gazing at an odd creature from behind a glass.

segments.text: All his life, Owen's been a quiet kid, not sullen, but just rather silent. When he was a baby and I'd be pushing him around in his stroller, people would stop and crouch down and talk to him and expect him to laugh and smile. And all he'd do was sigh and stare at them.

segments.speaker: Miriam Toews
segments.text: When he got a little older and went over to his friends' places to play and it was time for him to go home, he just got up and walked right out the door to the car. He didn't say, hey, thanks for having me or next time we'll play at my place or even goodbye. We'd be driving home. And I'd be trying to explain to him that it seemed rude and that sometimes we just had to say certain things at certain times. It was polite and expected.

segments.text: He'd just sigh and nod and kick the dash or stick his head entirely out the window. segments.speaker: Miriam Toews
segments.text: When he was eight and angry and sitting in a tree and throwing stones at the car or something, I'd go outside, knowing it would be a matter of minutes before he'd start to cry and then slowly spill his guts about whatever series of events it was that led to his meltdown, and that the whole scene would end with hugs and apologies and probably a large muscle activity, like him cheerfully taking shots at my head with a soccer ball. Now, though, the signs are harder, if not impossible, to read. I'm not sure there are any, actually. And I had no idea where to begin my search.

segments.text: I had wanted to learn more about him from his music. I was pretty sure his lyrics would tell me more about him than he would. segments.text: I realize my kids sound like boy and girl stereotypes. Owen is taciturn and into sports, and Georgia is chatty and prone to the occasional crying jag. But it really just is that way. segments.text: Sure. Yeah.

segments.speaker: Miriam Toews
segments.text: You envy that?

segments.speaker: Owen Toews
segments.text: I definitely envy that.

segments.speaker: Miriam Toews
segments.text: We were all pretty quiet as we drove up to Colorado Springs on our way to Denver. The sun was shining, but it was raining a bit. And we saw, not one, not two, but three dead cows in fields, stiff with their legs in the air. And it bothered us.

segments.speaker: Miriam Toews
segments.text: After the third dead cow, I played my favorite song of the summer, Gillian Welch's "Elvis Presley Blues." It's a wistful song about the King as a 15-year-old boy just starting out with a big rock-and-roll dream and a shirt his mother made. And it was kind of miraculous, because Owen actually liked it, too.

segments.speaker: Miriam Toews
segments.text: For me, it was a song about a boy becoming a man and leaving home. And it made me a little sad. I think Owen was probably hearing it as a song about a cool 15-year-old who was about to conquer the world. But really, I haven't got a clue how he heard the song or how it made him feel. All he said was that it had a decent pop sensibility. And then he was quiet.

segments.speaker: Miriam Toews
segments.text: These days, the more I press him for information, the faster he shuts right down. The other day, I tried a new approach-- his. I was annoyed by a bunch of things. And rather than broadcast it all over the house, I sat on the couch and glared at the TV and sighed periodically.

segments.speaker: Miriam Toews
segments.text: And strangely, Owen responded. He observed my weirdness for a while and then left. Then he came back and looked at me again and said one word-- "Mom"-- but in such a nice way that I smiled and said, Owen. And that was it. And then we sat there for a while, silently. I was surprised by how completely comfortable it felt. And then, finally, wordlessly, he got up and took his laundry upstairs.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Miriam Toews, she's a writer in Toronto. Her son, Owen, is now a grown man and Miriam tells us is long past his taciturn days. Her latest book is called A Truce That is Not Peace.
